response.text:
Baffled, Tommy strolled into the restaurant and ordered a meal of surpassing excellence. His four days' imprisonment had taught him anew to value good food.

He was conveying a particularly choice morsel of Sole à la Jeanette to his mouth when Julius entered. At sight of him, Julius's eyes seemed to pop out of his head.

"Holy snakes! Is it really you?"

"Of course. Why shouldn't it be?"

"Say, man, don't you know you've been given up for dead? Where's Tuppence?"

"Isn't she here? The fellows at the office said she'd just gone out."

"I dropped her here in the car about an hour ago. Fire ahead. I guess you've had some few adventures."

Tommy plunged into his recital. Julius listened spellbound. Then, in his turn, he narrated his own — Bournemouth, the buying of the car, the call upon Sir James, and the sensational occurrences of the previous night.

"But who killed her?" asked Tommy.

"The doctor kidded himself she took it herself," replied Julius dryly. He went on to detail the events of the morning — Jane's lost memory.

"Lost her memory, eh? By Jove, that explains why they looked at me so queerly when I spoke of questioning her."

"Mr. Brown?" hazarded Tommy.

"Sure thing."

"All the same, Mr. Brown hasn't got wings. Let's go round to the scene of the crime. I wish we could get hold of Tuppence."

Inquiry at the office revealed she had not yet returned. Julius went upstairs to look. Suddenly a diminutive boy spoke at Tommy's elbow.

"The young lady — she's gone away by train, I think, sir. The taxi. I heard her tell the driver Charing Cross and to look sharp."

"When?"

"When I took her the telegram, sir. About half-past twelve. She opened it and gave a gasp, and then she said, very jolly like: 'Bring me up a Bradshaw, and an A.B.C., and look sharp, Henry.' My name isn't Henry, but——"

"Never mind your name. Go on."

"She looked something up, then said 'Tell them to get me a taxi,' and she was down in two ticks."

Julius rejoined them. Tommy turned to him.

"Tuppence has gone off sleuthing on her own. She went off in a taxi to Charing Cross in the deuce of a hurry after getting a telegram."

"Hi — Henry! Do you remember what the young lady did with the telegram?"

"She crumpled it up and threw it into the grate, and made a sort of noise like 'Whoop!' sir."

They hurried upstairs. In the fireplace was a crumpled ball of orange and white. Tommy smoothed it out.

"Come at once, Moat House, Ebury, Yorkshire, great developments — TOMMY."

They looked at each other in stupefaction.

"You didn't send it?"

"Of course not."

"I guess it means the worst. They've got her. They signed your name, and she fell into the trap like a lamb."

"My God! What shall we do?"

"Get busy, and go after her! Right now!"

Tommy consulted an A.B.C. "Ebury, Yorks. From King's Cross. 12.50, that's the train she went by. 3.20 is the next — and a damned slow train too."

"I say, Julius, what do they want her for, anyway? I don't think it's their game to do her any harm. She's a hostage. As long as they've got her, they've got the whip hand of us. Besides, I've great faith in Tuppence."

Ebury proved a deserted station. The Moat House — a rusty iron gate swinging on its hinges, an overgrown drive thick with leaves, shutters closed, steps up to the door overgrown with moss — had a chill about it that struck both their hearts. The bell jangled discordantly through the emptiness within. No one came. Inquiry in the village confirmed it: empty for years. They were turning to leave when Tommy stooped among the leaves and held out a small gold brooch.

"That's Tuppence's. I've often seen her wear it."

"I guess that settles it. She came as far as here. We'll raise hell round here until we find her."

For a week they did. Julius was like a hound on the leash, tracking down every car that had passed through on the fateful day. So well had the abduction been planned that the girl seemed literally to have vanished into thin air.

"Do you know how long we've been here?" Tommy asked one morning. "A week! And next Sunday is the 29th. Her life won't be worth an hour's purchase afterwards. The hostage game will be played out by then."

"I'm with you. I'm going right back to London to put the case in the hands of your British police. We fancied ourselves as sleuths. Sleuths! Scotland Yard for me! The professional always scores over the amateur in the end."

But the course of events was not to follow the plan Julius had laid down. Later in the day Tommy received a wire:

*"Join me Manchester Midland Hotel. Important news — JULIUS."*

At 7.30 that night Julius was on the platform.

"Is Tuppence found?"

Julius shook his head and handed him a telegraph form.

*"Jane Finn found. Come Manchester Midland Hotel immediately — PEEL EDGERTON."*

"Queer," said Julius thoughtfully. "I thought that lawyer chap had quit!"
